mcqs.question: Why is a server's average CPU utilization usually a poor choice of SLI, even though it's easy to measure?
options: It's too expensive to collect compared to other metrics
It can only be measured once per day
It doesn't reflect what a user actually experiences — a request can succeed and be fast regardless of CPU level
It's not compatible with error budgets
mcqs.explanation: A good SLI must be user-facing: it should reflect whether the user's request actually succeeded and was fast, not an internal resource stat. CPU utilization is easy and cheap to collect, but high CPU doesn't necessarily mean users are suffering, and low CPU doesn't guarantee they aren't.

mcqs.question: Which of these is the best-formed SLI for an API's reliability?
options: Total number of requests served per day
Average CPU usage across all API hosts
Number of servers currently running
Fraction of requests that complete successfully under 300ms, out of all valid requests
mcqs.explanation: A good SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events, capturing user-perceived success — the fraction of fast, successful requests does exactly that. Raw request counts and server counts don't measure quality of experience, and CPU usage is an internal resource metric, not a user-facing one.

mcqs.question: A team sets an SLO of 99.9% but an SLA of 99.5%. Why is the SLA deliberately looser than the SLO?
options: So that an internal SLO breach triggers action well before the looser SLA threatens contractual penalties
Because it's a mistake — SLA and SLO should always be set to the same number
Because SLAs are always measured over a shorter time window
Because SLAs only apply to free-tier customers
mcqs.explanation: The gap is intentional: breaching the tighter internal SLO gives engineering a warning and a reason to prioritize reliability work before ever approaching the looser, financially consequential SLA. Setting them equal would remove that early-warning margin, not improve anything.

mcqs.question: In the SLI → SLO → SLA chain, why does each layer typically sit looser (a lower reliability number) than the one before it?
options: Because measurement accuracy degrades at each layer
The growing gap is a safety margin, so internal problems surface and get fixed before they become external, contractual failures
It's arbitrary and has no functional purpose
Because SLAs are measured with different tooling than SLIs
mcqs.explanation: Each gap is a deliberate buffer: the SLO sits below the SLI's normal healthy range so you notice drift early, and the SLA sits below the SLO so a contractual breach is rarer than an internal one. It's a designed safety margin, not measurement noise or an accident of tooling.

mcqs.question: What's the concrete problem with setting a service's SLO to 100%?
options: It's illegal in most SLA contracts
It makes the SLI impossible to measure
It's unachievable in practice and leaves zero error budget, so any imperfection technically blocks every future launch
It requires doubling the monitoring infrastructure
mcqs.explanation: 100% is not physically achievable at scale, and setting it as the target means the error budget (100% minus the SLO) is zero — so the smallest blip forces a launch freeze under a strict reading of the policy. It's a policy and incentive problem, not a legal, measurement, or infrastructure one.

mcqs.question: A team's SLI, measured at the load balancer, shows 99.98% availability, but customer complaints about failed requests keep coming in. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The load balancer's metric must be miscalculated and needs a bug fix

The LB-measured SLI only sees requests that actually reach it — failures further upstream, like DNS issues, client-side timeouts, CDN edge errors, or mobile network problems, never register in that number even though users experience them
The customers must be complaining about an unrelated feature, not availability
99.98% is below any reasonable SLO, so the SLO itself must be set incorrectly
mcqs.explanation: The measurement point defines what the SLI can see: anything failing before a request reaches the load balancer is invisible to it, so a high LB-side number doesn't guarantee a good real user experience. Assuming a metric bug, unrelated complaints, or a bad SLO skips the more likely, structural explanation — a blind spot upstream of the measurement point.
